docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sensing: My board will utilize an FSR sensor for force data

Power: The board will be powered via a barrel jack from a battery or a wall outlet adapter into a voltage regulator.

Connector to Bus Node: I will utilize an 8-pin connector to the Hub Board for digital and analog.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Force Sensor (Force Sensing Subsystem)

Solution Pros Cons Interlink FSR 402 round force-sensing resistor$7.12/eachFSR 402 on DigiKey * Force range of about 0.2–20 N covers both an egg and a baseball* Low turn-on force detects first contact with fragile objects* Very thin, fits under a pad on the gripper finger* Full datasheet with force vs. resistance curves * Nonlinear output, needs calibration with known weights* Reading drifts slightly under a constant load* Small round sensing area, force must be centered on it

Rationale: The FSR 402's range (about 0.2–20 N) covers our full target of 0.5–15 N, from light contact with an egg to a firm grip on a baseball. It is thin enough to mount on the gripper finger and has a full manufacturer datasheet for designing and calibrating the voltage divider circuit.

Op-Amp (Signal Conditioning Subsystem)

Solution Pros Cons Microchip MCP6004-I/P quad op-amp$0.59/eachMCP6004 on DigiKey * Rail-to-rail input and output, uses the full 0–5 V ADC range* Runs directly off our single 5 V rail* Four op-amps in one chip cover the gain stage and the low-pass filter* Through-hole package, already in our kit * Input offset up to about 4.5 mV (removed by the tare button)* 14-pin package takes more board space* Unused op-amps must be tied off

Rationale: The MCP6004 runs on our single 5 V rail, and its rail-to-rail output lets the signal use almost the full 0–5 V ADC range. One chip covers both analog stages, the gain stage (×1.5) and the Sallen-Key low-pass filter, and the two unused op-amps are tied off with pull-down resistors.

5V Voltage Regulator (Power Subsystem)

Solution Pros Cons LM7805 5 V 1.5 A linear regulator, TO-220$0.75/eachLM7805 on Adafruit * Accepts 7–35 V, covers the required 9–12 V input* 1.5 A output, far more than our board needs* Built-in current limiting and overheat protection* Through-hole and well documented * Needs at least 7 V input to stay regulated* Turns extra input voltage into heat* Uses about 6 mA just to stay on

Rationale: The LM7805 meets the course requirements for a through-hole linear regulator that accepts 9–12 V and outputs 5 V. With our 9 V wall adapter and the 1N4007 reverse-polarity diode, the regulator sees about 8.3 V, above its 7 V minimum, and gives off only about 0.2 W of heat, so no heatsink is needed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The schematic design and my board is responsible for force data utilizing the FSR-402 pressure sensor. The FSR sensor I chose is a variable resistor that increases conductivity upon pressure exertion. I am utilizing a voltage divider to output an analog voltage which rises as the sensor is pressed more. There is a second-stage op-amp circuit (MCP6004) for signal conditioning and implementation of a low-pass filter. After the op-amp stage the signal goes to ADC via my PIC's RA0 pin. I also have a tare button to zero force reading via our firmware, LEDs and extra pins for debugging, and the 8-pin connector for Hub Board.
